tldr: By using a bilinear Koopman operator, the proposed method reduces dynamics rollout predictions to simple matrix-vector multiplications, enabling noise-annealed model-based diffusion (MBD) trajectory optimization to run in real time within the control period. In both simulation and physical manipulator experiments, it achieved high-precision real-time tracking while staying well within a 50 ms control period.
hero_caption: Processing flow of BK-MBD within a single control step. The current state is lifted into a high-dimensional space only once using a neural network. Thereafter, all candidate trajectory rollouts across every annealing stage are executed rapidly using only bilinear matrix-vector multiplications.
overview:
Model-based diffusion (MBD) is a powerful trajectory optimization method that leverages noise annealing to produce excellent trajectories even under non-convex costs and constraints. However, evaluating repeated rollouts of the plant dynamics across numerous candidate controls at every step incurs an immense computational cost, largely confining its use to offline settings and out of reach for real-time model predictive control (MPC).

To solve this, the authors turned to the Koopman operator, which embeds nonlinear dynamics into a higher-dimensional linear space. Once the state is lifted into this high-dimensional space, rollouts reduce to simple matrix-vector multiplications. However, standard linear Koopman models cannot capture configuration-dependent input gains (such as a manipulator's Jacobian), severely degrading control performance. Furthermore, approximation errors in learned surrogate models often trap planners in local minima. This paper introduces bilinear Koopman model-based diffusion (BK-MBD). By incorporating bilinear dynamics (products of state and input), it correctly handles configuration-dependent input gains, while the noise-annealing schedule in diffusion sampling overcomes local minima introduced by surrogate-model error.

The authors validated BK-MBD using a 7-DOF arm (Franka Research 3) and a quadrotor across simulation and physical tracking of an unknown moving target. BK-MBD completed its planning updates in at most 14.7 ms (median 11.0 ms) within a 50 ms control period, successfully reaching goals and tracking targets in every trial. While linear Koopman and convex-optimization baselines consistently failed or missed deadlines, BK-MBD was the only method that met both the tracking task and the real-time deadline.
contributions: Introduced a bilinear Koopman model that lifts the state once per control step and reduces all candidate rollouts to matrix operations, enabling diffusion-based trajectory optimization (MBD) to run in real time on a CPU within a 50 ms control period.

Demonstrated both theoretically and empirically that a linear lift is structurally incapable of capturing configuration-dependent input gains essential for velocity-controlled robots, making a bilinear structure strictly necessary.

Revealed that the noise-annealing schedule in diffusion models overcomes not only the multimodality of the true cost function, but also spurious local minima arising from surrogate-model approximation error.

Demonstrated on a physical Franka Research 3 tracking an initially unknown moving target that BK-MBD was the only method to achieve the tracking task while meeting control deadlines, whereas baselines failed or missed deadlines.

sections.heading: Why hasn't diffusion-based MPC run in real time?
sections.summary: While MBD offers powerful search capabilities, the heavy cost of candidate rollouts has prevented real-time control. Koopman-based surrogates are promising, but face two key obstacles: representing configuration-dependent input gains and staying robust to surrogate-model error.
sections.details:
Sampling-based predictive controllers such as MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral) and MBD (Model-Based Diffusion) have gained significant attention for their flexibility in handling non-smooth, non-convex costs and constraints. In particular, MBD refines candidate trajectories from global exploration down to fine-grained tuning by gradually reducing noise through an annealing schedule.

However, running MBD in a receding-horizon control loop (MPC) in real time has been extremely difficult. At every control cycle, the planner must simulate and evaluate many candidate trajectories across all annealing stages. Even GPU-parallelized physics engines hit limits, and meeting control deadlines on a CPU requires an exceptionally lightweight surrogate model.

Lifting the state into a high-dimensional space via Koopman operator theory can reduce rollout calculations to simple matrix-vector multiplications. However, deploying a learned finite-dimensional Koopman model inside a sampling planner faces two major hurdles.

The first is the input representation hurdle. In conventional linear lifted models, the input gain matrix is constant. This fails to capture systems where input effectiveness varies dramatically with posture (such as velocity-controlled robot arms), corrupting the relative ranking of candidate trajectories. The second is the model error hurdle. Approximation errors in the learned surrogate model introduce spurious local minima on the surrogate cost landscape, trapping the planner.

To overcome both obstacles, this paper proposes "BK-MBD," combining a bilinear Koopman model with MBD's annealed sampling. The bilinear formulation naturally captures configuration-dependent input gains, while noise annealing escapes surrogate-induced local minima, resolving both challenges simultaneously.

sections.heading: Problem setup, MBD, and Koopman lifting fundamentals
sections.summary: This section formulates the tracking problem for control-affine systems, reviews MBD update rules and sampling properties, and compares linear versus bilinear Koopman rollouts for fast prediction.
sections.details:
### II-A Problem Formulation
This work targets velocity-controlled, control-affine systems $\dot{s}=f_{c}(s)+G(s)u$. Discretized with control period $\Delta t$, the tracking output $y=h(s)$ responds as $y_{t+1} - y_t \approx \Delta t(\omega(s_t) + \Phi(s_t)u_t)$. Here, $\Phi(s) = \nabla h\, G$ is the state- (configuration-) dependent input gain, and its variation across the workspace plays a critical role.

### II-B Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) Update Rule
MBD samples from a Boltzmann distribution based on a trajectory evaluation cost $J(U)$. Following a noise schedule $\sigma_1 > \cdots > \sigma_S$, it sequentially descends through Gaussian-smoothed targets. At stage $j$, $N$ candidates $U_k = U + \sigma_j \varepsilon_k$ are drawn around the current nominal control sequence, and the sequence updates via a cost-weighted average $U \leftarrow \sum_k w_k U_k$. This generalizes the MPPI update rule; with a single fixed noise level, it coincides with MPPI. A full control step requires $N \times S \times T$ rollouts.

### II-C Linear and Bilinear Koopman Rollouts
The observed state $b$ is lifted to a higher dimension $z = \Psi_\theta(b) \in \mathbb{R}^r$ using a neural network. While a linear model takes the form $z^+ = Az + Bu$, a bilinear model is expressed as $z^+ = Az + \sum_i u_i B_i z + B_0 u = M(u)z + B_0 u$. The derivative of the bilinear model with respect to input, $\partial z^+ / \partial u_i = B_0 e_i + B_i z$, depends on state $z$, naturally capturing configuration-dependent responses. Both models execute rollouts via size-$r$ matrix-vector multiplications, maintaining nearly identical computational complexity.

sections.heading: BK-MBD: Fusing bilinear rollouts with noise annealing
sections.summary: This section theoretically proves why linear lifting is insufficient, details a horizon-aware training loss, and explains how noise annealing mitigates surrogate-model errors.
sections.details:
### III-A Bilinear Rollouts and Input-Gain Expressiveness
With a linear model $z^+ = Az + Bu$, the predicted input gain for the output reduces to a single constant matrix $C_y B$ across the entire workspace. By Lemma 1, whenever the true input gain $\Phi(s)$ varies across the workspace, the maximum error between the linear model's predicted gain and the true gain is bounded below by at least half the maximum variation $\nu_\Phi$ of the true gain. Thus, no matter how large the feature dimension $r$ is, this error cannot be eliminated structurally.

In contrast, the bilinear model's predicted input gain is $C_y(B_0 + [B_1 z, \dots, B_m z])$, varying affinely with the lifted state $z$. It effortlessly captures input gains formed by products of trigonometric functions, such as robot Jacobians. Computationally, the planner lifts the current measured state only once (via neural network inference), performing all subsequent candidate rollouts strictly via bilinear matrix operations to keep control-loop latency minimal.

### III-B Horizon-Aware Identification
Standard Koopman identification minimizes one-step prediction errors. However, the planner rolls out trajectories over a horizon of $T$ steps to evaluate cumulative costs. Even small one-step errors can cause catastrophic drift over longer horizons. Therefore, the proposed method trains end-to-end on trajectory segments of planning horizon length $T$, combining a cumulative squared error loss on reconstructed features with a latent-space consistency regularizer.

### III-C The Role of Annealing under Surrogate Models
Learned surrogate models inevitably retain residual errors $\Delta J$. In fixed-noise samplers, small noise traps the plan in local minima, whereas large noise permits only coarse updates. An annealed schedule explores a smoothed global landscape during early high-noise stages, then refines the output during late low-noise stages. This drastically cuts the risk of becoming trapped in surrogate-induced local minima.

sections.heading: Thorough validation in simulation and on a physical FR3
sections.summary: Experiments validate the need for a bilinear structure, computational speed well below the 50 ms control period, surrogate error mitigation via annealing, non-convex navigation, and physical dynamic tracking.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on a 7-DOF Franka Research 3 (FR3) arm and a quadrotor. Calculations targeted completion within a 50 ms control period on an Intel Core Ultra 5 225F CPU without GPU acceleration.

### IV-B Rollout Model Comparison and Computational Latency
In an FR3 end-effector reaching task (50 trials), the constant-gain linear Koopman baseline (DK-MBD) succeeded within a 1 cm tolerance in only 1/50 trials (median error of 0.248 m), showing no improvement even with higher lifted dimensions. In contrast, the proposed BK-MBD reached the goal in all 50/50 trials, perfectly matching an oracle rollout using the true physics engine (MBD-true).
Computationally, rolling out the true simulator required a median of 2598 ms, exceeding the 50 ms deadline in 100% of steps. BK-MBD finished in at most 14.7 ms (median 11.0 ms), respecting the control deadline on every single step.

### IV-C Effects of the Annealing Schedule
Across comparisons matching total sample counts, fixed-wide and fixed-narrow noise schedules (equivalent to MPPI) suffered lower success rates, whereas BK-MBD with annealing achieved 50/50. Furthermore, under exact physics rollouts, the narrow schedule also achieved 10/10, confirming that annealing's advantage stems from robustness to learned surrogate-model errors rather than intrinsic task multimodality.

### IV-D Navigation in Non-Convex Feasible Spaces
In a quadrotor task passing through a circular opening in a wall, a conventional bilinear controller using local convexification succeeded in only 10/50 trials, getting stuck before the wall. In contrast, sampling-based BK-MBD treated the wall as a simple cost penalty and cleanly navigated the opening in all 50/50 trials.

### IV-E Dynamic Tracking on a Physical Manipulator
On a physical FR3, the planner tracked a moving target describing an initially unknown circular path. Linear Koopman (DK-MBD) triggered safety stops due to gain mismatch under configuration changes, MBD-true could not move due to computational latency, and fixed-noise BK-MPPI exceeded tracking error limits mid-trajectory. BK-MBD was the only method that completed all 10 trials, consistently honoring the 50 ms period with a median latency of 22.9 ms (maximum 44.7 ms).

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: BK-MBD blends a bilinear Koopman model with annealed sampling to realize accurate diffusion-based MPC on a CPU in real time. Extending the approach to contact-rich tasks remains an important future challenge.
sections.details:
This work proposed "BK-MBD," which leverages a data-driven bilinear Koopman model to execute MBD's annealed sampling within real-time control periods. Through simulation experiments, the authors clearly isolated and validated three key factors: input-gain expressiveness in rollout models, noise annealing's effectiveness against surrogate errors, and the ability to traverse non-convex feasible spaces.

In physical manipulator experiments, it stood as the only method that met both the dynamic target tracking task and the control deadline.

However, all tasks evaluated in this paper were non-contact motions in free space. A compelling open challenge is whether the discontinuous dynamics of contact-rich manipulation—where MBD naturally excels—can be lifted and captured effectively using Koopman operators.

takeaways: When identifying Koopman operators for velocity-controlled robots, linear models cannot capture configuration-dependent input gains (such as Jacobians), causing sampling searches to fail; a bilinear model is indispensable.

By lifting the state only once per control step and evaluating all subsequent rollouts via matrix operations, diffusion-based MPC runs entirely on a CPU (taking at most ~15 ms against a 50 ms deadline) without heavy physics engines.
Noise annealing in diffusion models serves as a strong defense against surrogate errors, escaping local minima introduced by learned model inaccuracies in addition to enabling global search.
Using sampling-based optimization preserves bilinear dynamics without local linearization or convex approximations, naturally handling non-convex obstacle avoidance.
limitations: Evaluations were restricted to non-contact motions; how well bilinear Koopman models can capture dynamic discontinuities and impacts during contact remains unverified.
Training the bilinear model relies on domain knowledge to pre-incorporate specific features, such as trigonometric functions, into the feature map.
Physical validation was limited to velocity control on a 7-DOF arm; scaling to higher-DOF humanoid robots or torque-controlled systems remains to be verified.
